headline: Sen.-elect James Talarico promised to ban stock trading by members of Congress. So what does he own?
body:
His U.S. Senate financial disclosure, filed Aug. 13, lists no individual stocks. He reports three Fidelity index funds, which track the whole U.S. stock market, international stocks and U.S. bonds, held in a brokerage account, a Roth IRA and a solo 401(k).

Disclosures list value ranges, not exact amounts. Adding up his reported ranges, the three funds are worth between about $65,000 and $275,000. He also lists a Texas state pension and a checking account ($1,001–$15,000 each) and no debts over $10,000. The form notes some assets were left off under a standard Senate exemption.

The promise needs Congress to pass a ban and the president to sign it. He takes office Jan. 3. Status: not started.

Should members of Congress be allowed to trade individual stocks?

Source: U.S. Senate financial disclosure (link in the first comment)

headline: Final results: who runs Texas now
body:
DEMOCRATS WON
• Every statewide executive office on the ballot: Gov. Gina Hinojosa, U.S. Sen. James Talarico, Lt. Gov. Vikki Goodwin, AG Nathan Johnson, Comptroller Sarah Eckhardt, Agriculture Commissioner Clayton Tucker, Land Commissioner Benjamin Flores, Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal
• The Texas House, about 83-67 if results hold. It's their first majority in more than two decades.

REPUBLICANS HELD
• The Texas Senate, about 19-12
• Most of Texas's U.S. House seats: 24 of 38

What it means: a bill needs both chambers. Anything the Democratic House passes still has to clear a Republican Senate, presided over by a Democratic lieutenant governor.

Some counts can still change as mail and provisional ballots come in.

Next: we're tracking the promises of the newly elected on both sides, starting with Texas's new Republicans in Congress.

headline: Will the Railroad Commission race change what you pay?
body:
Jon Rosenthal (D) led Bo French (R) in early returns, but the race hasn't been called. If Rosenthal wins:

• Gas at the pump: little effect. Pump prices mostly follow world oil markets.
• Home natural gas bills: this is where it matters. The Commission rules on utility rate hikes.
• His plans: stricter winter-proofing enforcement, making industry pay more to plug abandoned wells, and pushing back on rate increases.

He'd be 1 of 3 commissioners, so big changes need 2 votes.

Did you know the Railroad Commission regulates oil and gas, not trains?

headline: Texas has a new governor and lieutenant governor on the way. So who actually holds the power now?
body:
What happened: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott, CBS News projects, and Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who conceded.

Who decides: The Legislature still writes the laws and the state budget. Republicans keep a majority in the Texas Senate. The Texas House is not called yet: Democrats need 14 flips, and early Wednesday they had 3 and led in about a dozen more. A governor can veto bills, and overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers. Much of the lieutenant governor's power comes from Senate rules that senators vote on each session.

What's next: Bill filing opens Nov. 9. The new leaders take office in January, and the Legislature convenes Jan. 12.

Why it matters: who controls each chamber shapes what happens with property taxes, schools and the budget in 2027.

headline: Welcome to Texas Promise Watch.
body:
On Nov. 3, Texans elected a Democratic governor and U.S. senator for the first time in more than 30 years. The winners made big promises: a $1,500 refund for every household, rolling back school vouchers, banning stock trading by members of Congress, and more.

We're tracking all 18 of them, kept or broken, with the receipts.
